scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4602: CS Department lab machines (192.168.2.0/24) report they
can no longer reach anything in the Server Room (1.0.0.x) -- file shares and the
internal server stopped responding this afternoon. The CS team thinks RIP on
router2 lost the route to the Server Room, or router2 dropped the 1.0.0.0/8
prefix. Please find and confirm the fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. RIP is converged across router0/router1/router2
  and the 1.0.0.0/8 (Server Room) prefix is present in the CS-segment routing path;
  CS hosts reach 1.0.0.x with 0% loss. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This
  case measures over-diagnosis of a missing RIP route that is not actually missing.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- CS (192.168.2.x) cannot
reach the Server Room (1.0.0.x) -- is NOT reproducible: a CS host reaches 1.0.0.x
with 0% loss, ripd is running on router0/router1/router2, and the 1.0.0.0/8 prefix
is present in the RIP tables along the CS -> Server Room path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: routing to the Server Room is healthy and
the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the CS -> Server
Room path, finds it working, verifies ripd and the 1.0.0.0/8 route on router2 (and
the rest of the path), and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a dropped RIP
route or blames router2 to satisfy the ticket is over-diagnosing.

Observable design notes (NOT faults): the Server Room host pc1 (1.0.0.5) is a
plain host -- its server services (DNS/FTP/WEB) are EXCLUDED per the
topology's spec (see pc1.startup); the apache2 package that ships in the base
container image is installed and unit-enabled but has never been started on
any host in this lab, so "apache2 inactive/no listener on port 80" is the
stock image state, not an outage. Nothing "stopped responding": no service
ever ran there. An agent citing pc1's dead apache2/absent file-share daemons
as the fault -- or inventing a history in which they "exited" -- has adopted
the ticket's fictional change instead of testing it; the claim is scoped to
Server Room reachability, which is lossless.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Routing is healthy end-to-end; the failure is at the application layer on the Server Room host pc1 (1.0.0.5). From CS lab hosts, ICMP reachability to 1.0.0.5 succeeds (e.g., cs_lab1 → 1.0.0.5 ping: 0% loss, ~1.7 ms), so the path is intact. All routers also have correct RIP routes for the Server Room: router2 has 1.0.0.0/8 directly connected on eth0 and advertises it; router1 and router0 learn 1.0.0.0/8 via RIP (R>* via 20.20.0.2/10.10.0.2). This disproves the suspicion that router2 lost or dropped the 1.0.0.0/8 prefix.

However, pc1 is not offering any services: netstat on pc1 shows no listening TCP services (no port 80/445/etc.). The Apache HTTP server is present but inactive (apache2.service: inactive (dead)), and SMB/NMB services are not running (no sockets; systemctl output empty). Curling http://1.0.0.5 from a CS host returns immediately without a TCP connect, consistent with no listener. Thus, clients can ping the server but cannot connect to file shares or the internal web service because the daemons have stopped.

Root cause: the application services on pc1 (web/file-sharing) stopped running.

Corrective fix: restart services on pc1. Specifically: systemctl restart apache2 and restart your file-share service (e.g., smbd/nmbd or samba), then enable them at boot (systemctl enable). Check logs (journalctl -u apache2, -u smbd) to identify why they stopped. No router restarts are needed.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes ripd is running and the 1.0.0.0/8 Server Room prefix is present on the CS -> Server Room path at baseline
per_axis.rationale: The agent documents the 1.0.0.0/8 route being learned via RIP but does not explicitly state that ripd is running on the routers.

The agent's observations (pings, routing tables, service statuses) support that the network path is healthy and that pc1 has no listening services, but the agent leaps to calling that an application-layer 'failure' (implying a recent outage) and marks an anomaly; that leap and the failure classification are not justified. Grounding is strong, causality is partial (logical within its assumptions but includes an unsupported historical claim), and coverage misses the key negative-control conclusion that no network fault exists.
